papers.version_note: arXiv:2501.05046v1 [math.OC], 9 Jan 2025. The text layer loses the math symbols (they print as replacement characters), so equations (1) to (5), the Table 3 values and some table row labels are not reliably quotable; figures 1 to 3 are images and only their captions were read.
papers.what_it_is: A short conference-style paper that casts a six-step, seven-node space logistics problem as a multicommodity network flow, turns it into a penalty Hamiltonian, and reports 40 samples from QCi's Dirac-3 entropy quantum computing device.

assertions.value: The authors state that the case study is a hypothetical scenario involving orbital locations such as Earth, Low Earth Orbit (LEO), Lunar Transfer Orbit (LTO), Low Lunar Orbit (LLO), Lunar Surface (LS), Low Mars Orbit (LMO) and Mars.

Low Earth Orbit (LEO)
Lunar Transfer Orbit (LTO)
Low Lunar Orbit (LLO)
Lunar Surface (LS)
Low Mars Orbit (LMO)
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.A states the scenario of the only experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: The scenario is hypothetical, so the experiment does not test a real mission.

assertions.value: The authors state that the cost parameter of each arc is the velocity change required to traverse the arc, measured in kilometers per second, and that the time of flight is fixed and equal to 1 for all arcs.
quotes: representing the velocity change required to traverse the arc.
measured in kilometers per second (Km/s)
is fixed and equal to 1 for all arcs, simplifying the formulation and ensuring consistency across the network.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.A states the cost and time-of-flight setup.
assertions.reader_inference: A fixed time of flight of 1 removes the time-delay structure of the general formulation from the test.

assertions.value: The authors set Earth as origin; LEO, LTO, LLO and LMO as intermediate; and Lunar Surface and Mars as destinations, with the Earth row carrying supply entries (+40, +80) and (+60, +120) and the destination rows carrying demand entries (−20, −40) and (−30, −60).
quotes: Origin Intermediate Intermediate Intermediate Destination Intermediate Destination
assertions.certainty_reason: Table 1 states the supply and demand of the only experiment.
assertions.reader_inference: Total supply equals total demand for each commodity (100 and 200 units), and the row positions give the time steps.

assertions.value: The authors formulate space logistics as a time-expanded multi-commodity network flow problem on a directed graph of depots and directed routes, with the objective of optimizing the transportation of multiple commodities through a capacitated network.
quotes: with the objective of optimizing the transportation of multiple commodities through a capacitated network
nodes represent orbits, planets, or celestial objects, and arcs denote the trajectories linking the nodes.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section III.A defines the model the results depend on.
assertions.reader_inference: Equations (1) to (4) are in the text layer only as fragments; the model is a standard integer-flow, vehicle-capacity cost minimization.

assertions.value: The authors state that spacecraft, crew, scientific instruments and other payloads (for example water, food, oxygen, propellent) are all regarded as commodities traversing the arcs, citing earlier work.
quotes: The spacecraft, crew, scientific instruments, and other payloads (e.g., water, food, oxygen, propellent) are all regarded as the commodities traversing the arcs [9].
assertions.certainty_reason: The modelling convention is attributed to reference 9.

assertions.value: The authors state that entropy quantum computing was introduced recently as an efficient optimization technique that leverages the principles of entropy minimization to guide quantum state evolution toward optimal solutions of a Hamiltonian, citing reference 10.
quotes: Entropy quantum computing was introduced recently as an efficient optimization technique that leverages the
principles of entropy minimization to guide quantum state evolution toward optimal solutions of a Hamiltonian [10].
assertions.certainty_reason: A company author team describes its own technique and cites its own paper.
assertions.reader_inference: Reference 10 shares authors with this paper (Miri, Rupert, Dyk), so the description is not independent.

assertions.value: The authors describe a photonic realization in which qudits are encoded as a superposition of photon numbers in time bins that evolve in an optical fiber loop which embeds a desired Hamiltonian as a dissipative operator, emulating imaginary time evolution.
quotes: qudits are encoded as a superposition of photon numbers in time bins that evolve in an optical fiber loop which embeds a desired Hamiltonian as a dissipative operator.
This effectively emulates imaginary time evolution
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' company describes how its own device works.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current generation of EQC hardware at QCi, named Dirac-3, is a hybrid system that combines the high-speed parallel processing capabilities of photonics and the quantum nature of light with the precise control and programmability of electronic circuits.
quotes: named Dirac-3, is a hybrid system that harnesses the high-speed parallel processing capabilities of photonics and the quantum nature of light with the precise control and programmability of electronic circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own product.

assertions.value: The authors state that such hybrid systems can explore large solution spaces rapidly through photonic modes propagation, and that this offers a pathway for challenging optimization problems with the potential for high speed, low power consumption, and scalability.
quotes: Such systems can explore large solution spaces rapidly through photonic modes propagation
with the potential for high speed, low power consumption, and scalability.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor states potential benefits of its own product without a measurement in this section.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper reports no comparison of speed, power or scaling with any other solver.

assertions.value: The authors state that Dirac-3 targets optimization of a polynomial objective function with linear terms and two-body to fifth-body interaction coefficients that are real numbers, the interaction tensors being symmetric under all permutations of the indices.
quotes: The EQC hardware Dirac-3 targets optimization of a polynomial objective function
two-body to fifth-body interaction coefficients that are real numbers subject to the tensors
being symmetric under all permutations of the indices.

assertions.value: The authors state that a major advantage of EQC compared to other quantum annealers is its flexible variable encoding capability, and that by allocating multiple photon time bins to one variable one can effectively encode binary or integer variables.
quotes: A major advantage of EQC compared to other quantum annealers is its flexible variable encoding capability [10].

assertions.value: The authors report that their Python code formulates the objective as a vector and all constraints as a linear system of equalities, and turns the constraints into penalties that form a polynomial of order 2 as done for QUBO in reference 11.
quotes: all the constraints from the model description as a linear system of equalities
These constraints become penalties,
a polynomial of order 2 just as is done for QUBO in [11].
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B states how the experiment's Hamiltonian is built.
assertions.reader_inference: The capacity inequality (3) must therefore enter through slack variables, which fits the 29 slack variables reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the penalty multiplier is chosen to elevate the penalties above the objective function coefficients, and that increasing it separates feasible from infeasible solutions in energy but can reduce the impact of small objective coefficients.
quotes: is a multiplier that is chosen to elevate the penalties enough to make positive penalties greater than the objective function coefficients.

Increasing this value provides more separation of feasible solutions from infeasible ones in terms of energy value, but this also can reduce the impact of small coefficients in the objective function.
assertions.certainty_reason: A design statement without evidence in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors define the dynamic range of a problem as the ratio of the largest to the smallest absolute magnitude in the problem, reported in decibels, and give the example that a ratio of 200 is about 23dB.
quotes: The ratio of the magnitudes of the largest to the smallest absolute values in the problem is called the dynamic range of the problem and is reported in decibels.
if the ratio is 200, then the dynamic range is log10 200 ≈ 23dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B defines the term used for the hardware limit.
assertions.reader_inference: 23 dB for a ratio of 200 matches 10 times log10 of 200, not log10 alone as printed; the decibel convention is power-style 10 log10.

assertions.value: The authors report that the Hamiltonian has 116 variables, 89 of which are decision variables and 29 are slack variables, with 331 levels in total, each a time dimension in Dirac-3, and that its coefficients have a dynamic range of 30.78 dB.
quotes: has 116 variables, 89 of which are decision variables and 29 are slack variables.
Among all variables, there are 331 levels, each a time dimension in Dirac-3.
The coefficients have a dynamic range of 30.78 dB.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV.B states the size of the model the device ran.
assertions.reader_inference: A problem of 116 variables is small enough that a classical exact solver would solve it; the paper reports no classical baseline.

assertions.value: The authors report that each sample took between 2.44 and 2.61 seconds of device and post processing time, 2.53 seconds on average, with about 1.5 seconds of device time and about 1 second of post processing per sample.

assertions.value: The authors report that the raw solution contained spurious commodity movements, which prompted a post-processing method that set all commodity flows to 0 when no vehicle was scheduled, without modifying the vehicle schedule determined by the device.
quotes: The raw solution contained a single load of
This prompted the inclusion of a post-processing method which set all commodity flows to 0 when no vehicle was scheduled (negligible to runtime).
This eliminated the spurious movements of commodities with no supply or demand, while not modifying the vehicle schedule determined by the device.
assertions.certainty_reason: An observation from one run.
assertions.reader_inference: The reported solution is therefore not the device's raw output; the device chose the vehicle schedule and a classical step cleaned the cargo flows.

assertions.certainty_reason: A single result from one instance.

assertions.value: The authors state that space logistics missions often have an exponential growth of the solution space that classical methods cannot efficiently solve.
quotes: often resulting in an exponential growth of the solution space that classical methods cannot efficiently solve.
assertions.certainty_reason: An abstract statement without evidence in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper cites classical approaches (piecewise linear approximation, reinforcement learning, decomposition) in the introduction but does not test any against the quantum run.

assertions.value: The authors state that they discretize the problem space with a Hamiltonian-based system state representation and that they can perform adiabatic quantum optimization (AQO) to identify the optimal system Hamiltonian that optimizes the logistics planning.
quotes: We discretize the problem space by proposing a Hamiltonian-based system state representation
Then, we can perform adiabatic quantum optimization (AQO) to identify the optimal system Hamiltonian that optimizes the logistics planning.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of intent in the introduction.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiments use Dirac-3 entropy computing, not adiabatic quantum optimization, so the introduction describes a different method from the one run.

assertions.value: The authors state that this paper will be one of the first attempts to bring quantum computing in solving large-scale space logistics planning problems.
quotes: This paper will be one of the first attempts to bring quantum computing in solving large-scale space logistics planning problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim without a survey in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The instance (seven nodes, six steps, 116 variables) is small next to the phrase large-scale.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the results validate the feasibility of quantum-assisted frameworks in optimizing logistical networks that are intractable for classical methods, and that the use of entropy quantum computing allowed the simultaneous evaluation of multiple solutions with the potential to significantly reduce computation time.
quotes: The results validate the feasibility of quantum-assisted frameworks in optimizing logistical networks that are intractable for classical methods.
with the potential to significantly reduce computation time
assertions.certainty_reason: A conclusion not supported by a classical baseline or a scaling test in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The experiment is one small instance, the reported solution is not optimal by the authors' own statement, and no classical runtime or solution is given. The claim about networks intractable for classical methods is not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state that future work will focus on enhancing the scalability of the approach with advanced quantum algorithms and hardware, and on exploring its applicability to broader domains such as terrestrial logistics and supply chain optimization.
quotes: Future work will focus on enhancing the scalability of the approach with advanced quantum algorithms and hardware
such as terrestrial logistics and supply chain optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V states scalability as open work.
assertions.reader_inference: Naming scalability as future work implies it was not shown here.
